top.title: 3 Observations from Indiana men’s basketball’s 90-76 win over Kentucky
top.description: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - NOVEMBER 20: Markus Burton #5 of the Indiana Hoosiers celebrates in the second half of the 90-76 win over the Kentucky Wildcats at Lucas Oil Stadium on November 20, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images Darian DeVries avenged his loss to Kentucky last season with a 14-point win in the rivalry series’ ‘semi-neutral’ game at Lucas Oil Stadium. Indiana remains perfect on the season while the Wildcats fall to 4-2 with lopsided losses to both high major programs they’ve seen this year. Indiana built an early lead in the game before Milan Momcilovic single-handedly brought Kentucky back from the dead. His 22-point first half was enough to kill Indiana’s momentum and give Kentucky a two point lead heading into halftime. DeVries knew that the key to the second half would be slowing him down and his group came out and did just that. Momcilovic didn’t make a three in the entire second half and Indiana finally built the lead that eluded them early in the game, eventually winning 90-76. Here are three observations from the game: Bryce Lindsay It’s not often that your most important player is a bench guy, but Bryce Lindsay is looking like the best sixth-man in the country and has been a huge difference-maker for Indiana’s perfect start. It starts with his willingness to come off the bench. Lindsay started all 31 games at Villanova last season and clearly has the ability to be a high-major starter. Whatever the conversation was to get him to accept this role at Indiana, the fit is a testament to both he and DeVries. Part of what has made this work so well is that he tends to share the floor with one of Darren Harris or Markus Burton, allowing him to alternate between shooter and driver. The other part of it is simply his ability to hit shots at all levels, often with more than one defender on him. His 3-point shooting will always be what jumps off the page, especially with the range he showed against Arkansas, but tonight showed his versatility inside. Kentucky knew it struggled to defend the perimeter, so he punished their overly aggressive close-outs with drives or by drawing fouls from beyond the arc. He’s going to miss some frustrating ones with the green light he has, but Lindsay has shown a willingness and ability to hit the hardest shots all over the floor. This is an invaluable piece to have coming off the bench. Versatility I’ve been waiting for this team to establish either an interior or perimeter offensive identity this season, but it turns out Indiana’s real strength might be its ability to do both. DeVries knew that he had the size and experience over Arkansas inside and fed Samet Yigitoglu and Aiden Sherrell inside accordingly. Malachi Moreno negated that advantage against Kentucky, so DeVries fell back on the guard play that helped him beat Syracuse. top.description: Heading into halftime, Kentucky Basketball had as much momentum as they have had at any point in any game all season. The Wildcats closed the half on a 12-0 run to lead Indiana 47-45 at halftime inside Lucas Oil Stadium. Milan Momcilovic was making it rain, and Kentucky’s defense was getting stops. Then, the script completely flipped in the second half. Kentucky’s defense couldn’t stop fouling, and the Wildcats’ offense couldn’t stop turning the ball over. It led to a frustrating second half where Indiana gradually and frustratingly pulled away for a 90-76 win. The curse in Indianapolis continues for the Cats. Kentucky is now 4-2 on the season and 0-2 against Power Four teams. Next up for the Cats: A home game next Friday night against Wichita State. MVP: Milan Momcilovic Easy. Momcilovic exploded for 22 points and five three-pointers in the first half. He finished with a game-high 28 points. He can shoot, clearly. Now we just need to see it in a Kentucky uniform for 40 minutes in a Power Four game. Box Score First Half It was an offensive explosion on both sides early. The first media timeout didn’t come until 12:50 left in the first half. By that point, it was 19-19. Both teams were 8-14 from the floor, with a combined 5-8 from three-point range. Kentucky had five assists to no turnovers in the first 7:10 of the game, and Milan Momcilovic had seven points and two three-pointers. From there, though, Indiana kept up their shot-making, hitting six-of-eight to stretch out an 11-point lead to 36-25. Part of that stretch included an 8-0 run over 52 seconds that saw three-pointers from the Hoosiers’ Bryce Lindsay and Markus Burton. Alex Wilkins responded with five points to give the Cats a 38-30 lead with 7:25 left in the first half. Kentucky was keeping it close, but where Indiana stayed in front was on offensive rebounding. Then again, it helps to have Milan Momcilovic. The best shooter in the country exploded late in the first half, sparking a 10-0 run with back-to-back three-pointers that tied the game 45-45 with 1:25 remaining. Momcilovic was explosive in the first half, scoring 22 points and hitting five-of-six three-pointers. He was 8-10 from the floor overall, and he also dished out two assists. Zoom Diallo hit a short jumper with seven seconds remaining to give Kentucky a 47-45 lead at halftime. With 10 points, Diallo was Kentucky’s other double-digit scorer in the first half. top.title: 'They should be willing to flip-flop': Mike Florio suggests Thanksgiving flex games
top.description: Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images, NBC Sports Next week’s slate of NFL games on Thanksgiving has a lot to like about it. In keeping with tradition, the Detroit Lions and Dallas Cowboys will both host a game on Turkey Day, while the third, rotating primetime game will be hosted by the Buffalo Bills. But it’s possible that one aspect of the traditional Thanksgiving Day schedule is due for a change. The Lions are always the early game on Thanksgiving, while the Cowboys kickoff around 4:30 p.m. ET. The simplest reason behind this fact is time zones, but because of the relative state of both teams and the importance of their upcoming games next Thursday, Mike Florio believes the time may be right for the NFL to embrace flexing its schedule on the holiday. This year, the Lions host the Chicago Bears in a game that will have huge ramifications in the NFC North, the best division in football by a healthy margin so far this season. The Cowboys, whose defense can’t do anything, are hosting the Philadelphia Eagles, who can’t do anything on either side of the ball. While that NFC East matchup was an easy sell on paper before the start of the season, it sure looks a lot less appealing now than it did in Week 1. Florio has high expectations for the Lions-Bears game, even if it is going to start early. “I think the ratings for that game are going to be through the roof. I’m starting to think it might even be larger than the 47.7 million from last year,” Florio said, referencing the massive rating the Lions brought in with their Thanksgiving game against the Packers in 2025. “People are going to appreciate the fact that the good game is the early game. The middle game, Eagles-Cowboys, who cares? If you want to see a good, compelling, dramatic football game, that’s the one. It used to be the other way around. How many years was the Lions game just, ‘That’s what’s on TV — somebody is rolling into Detroit to beat up the Lions, it’s going to be 23–6 in the fourth quarter, let’s just get this thing over with and let’s bring out the Cowboys’? The vibe has completely shifted.” Florio argued that given the league’s broad flex privileges when it comes to its primetime schedule, a similar ability should be established to allow the league to move the better Thanksgiving game into the afternoon slot. “Frankly, they flex everything else. They should be willing to flip-flop the Lions and Cowboys games. They should be willing to say, ‘Alright we’re starting the Cowboys game at basically 12:30 p.m. ET, and we’re going to delay the Lions game.’ You give people a week, two weeks notice. We would’ve known a week or two ago that Bears-Lions is the far more compelling game. If you want to blow out the number at 4:30 p.m. ET, you put Bears-Lions in that window.” The ratings for Bears-Lions on Thanksgiving will be through the roof. They’d be even bigger if the kickoff times for Bears-Lions and Eagles-Cowboys were flipped. https://t.co/LNn9rliQBn — PFT Live (@PFT_Live) November 19, 2026 W

top.title: Sandpapergate peace deal: AUS players' union chief urges shared responsibility, slams 'unacceptable' hounding of Pat Cummins
top.description: Sandpapergate peace deal: AUS players' union chief urges shared responsibility, slams 'unacceptable' hounding of Pat Cummins originally appeared on Cricket News . Add Cricket News as a Preferred Source by clicking here . KEY TAKEAWAYS: Australian Players’ Union boss Paul Marsh wants everyone linked to the 2018 tour to share blame. He also says the intrusion into Pat Cummins’ private life has gone too far. Marsh believes a shared acknowledgement could help the sport heal and move on. Paul Marsh calls on Pat Cummins and Cricket Australia to take collective responsibility to end Sandpapergate crisis A peace deal of sorts for the Sandpapergate saga is what Paul Marsh, the chief executive of the Australian Cricketers’ Association (ACA), is now proposing. He wants every member of the 2018 touring group in South Africa, Pat Cummins and the other fast bowlers included, to stand alongside Cricket Australia (CA) and accept collective responsibility for what happened. He has stayed in regular contact with Cummins, Usman Khawaja and other players and support staff from that period, former coach Darren Lehmann among them. Out of those conversations, Marsh has concluded that an admission of shared accountability offers the group its best chance of moving forward, even if some of those on the tour continue to deny any specific knowledge of sandpaper. The proposal arrives at a delicate moment, since the dispute over who knew what, and when, has split opinion inside the game and raised awkward questions about the Australian captain himself. The current tension traces back to 2021, when Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon put their names to a joint statement, where they insisted that they had no prior knowledge of sandpaper being “taken onto the field”. Cummins has since doubled down on his position, and he now says he had no knowledge of any ball tampering, either before the tour or during it. Those claims have now been challenged by Khawaja, David Warner, Chadd Sayers and Cameron Bancroft, and their accounts have fed a growing credibility problem for Australian cricket. The situation is made more sensitive by the ACA’s own makeup, because Khawaja is a current director of the body that Marsh leads. Cummins is a former director, and so is his manager, Neil Maxwell. top.title: Do women control their husbands?
top.description: By Chioma Gabriel, Editor, Special Features It is often said that women are a necessary evil, a desirable calamity and a domestic peril. It all depends on where one is standing. In traditional African societies, a woman’s place was said to be in the kitchen, from where she was expected to work her way into her husband’s heart through his stomach. Women were traditionally expected to be seen but not heard. They were like shadows trailing their husbands, with little or no opportunity to express opinions on matters affecting the family and society. They were often regarded as acquired possessions whose primary responsibilities were to bear children and provide labour on the farms. They had little or no say in the scheme of things. A similar pattern appears in some biblical accounts, where headcounts excluded women and children. When Jesus fed the 5,000 and the 4,000, the recorded figures referred to the men, with women and children excluded from the count. In the early Christian community, Paul’s instruction required women to remain silent in church and ask their husbands questions at home. Although interpretations of this passage differ among Christian scholars, it has historically been cited to support restrictions on women’s public religious participation. Despite these historical and cultural limitations, women have, in different ways, exercised considerable influence over men, including their husbands. Biblical accounts The Bible contains several accounts of women whose actions, decisions or influence significantly shaped the lives of men. Eve persuaded Adam to eat the forbidden fruit after the serpent tempted her in the Garden of Eden. Jezebel manipulated her husband, King Ahab, and orchestrated the murder of Naboth to acquire his vineyard. Delilah used persistent pressure and deception to make Samson reveal the secret of his extraordinary strength. Sapphira conspired with her husband, Ananias, to deceive the apostles about the proceeds from the sale of their property. Michal helped David escape from King Saul but later confronted and despised him over his public dancing before God. Bathsheba, working alongside the prophet Nathan, intervened to ensure that David fulfilled his promise that Solomon would succeed him as king. Sarah persuaded Abraham to have a child through her maidservant, Hagar, and later demanded that Hagar and Ishmael be sent away. Rebekah orchestrated a family deception by persuading her son Jacob to disguise himself as Esau and obtain Isaac’s blessing. Herodias influenced her daughter to demand the head of John the Baptist from her husband, Herod Antipas. Job’s wife, overwhelmed by their suffering, urged her husband to curse God and die. Mary and Martha also demonstrated the emotional influence women could have. When their brother, Lazarus, died, their grief deeply moved Jesus, who wept before raising him from the dead. top.description: Nets magic Team meetings. Lineup changes. Whatever it took. Brooklyn tried everything to shake up a three-game losing skid. The Nets finally showed some heart Friday night. But then they got it broken in a 113-111 loss to the Magic in front of a crowd of 17,067 at Barclays Center. Franz Wagner hit a go-ahead 14-footer with 2.8 seconds left, and Julius Randle missed a desperation 3-pointer at the buzzer on the other end. Brooklyn Nets forward Danny Wolf shoots as Orlando Magic center Wendell Carter Jr. defends on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, at Barclays Center in Brooklyn, N.Y. Robert Sabo for NY Post Randle finished with a team-high 27 points, and Brooklyn fought. They just couldn’t quite close. After the Nets (3-12) embarrassed themselves in Wednesday’s 137-107 non-effort against Chicago , they held a team meeting, with some real talk about what went wrong and how to fix it. Friday’s effort showed it wasn’t all just talk. It just wasn’t quite enough. “No one wants to lose like we did [Wednesday] … so a lot needed to be said. A lot of guys have been doing a lot of talking; we’ve all been doing a lot of talking,” Michael Porter Jr. said. “We’ve gotta string some games together. We’ve had spurts of good responses after really bad games, but that has to be a consistent theme. We can’t just let that be responses to really bad losses.” Wednesday qualified as a really bad loss, the worst of a disappointing season. top.description: (Photo by Guido De Bortoli/LAT Images) George Russell led the way in the third and final hour of practice at the Las Vegas Grand Prix Friday evening. But will the Mercedes driver top the timing sheets during the all-important qualifying hour later tonight? Russell led teammate Kimi Antonelli and McLaren’s Lando Norris in FP3 Friday evening, with the veteran Mercedes driver posting a lap of 1:34.041, almost a full second ahead of Antonelli, who was 0.911 seconds off the pace. Friday’s FP3 session was the only representative session of the weekend so far, as both FP1 and FP2 on Thursday were compromised by wet weather. The biggest story so far in Las Vegas might just be the list of drivers taking a grid penalty due to new components. Five drivers — Antonelli, Lance Stroll, Oliver Bearman, Oscar Piastri, and Carlos Sainz — have already taken on new components ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix and are facing grid drops at the start of the race. Antonelli is facing a five-place grid drop, while Stroll, Piastri, and Sainz are facing ten-place grid drops. Bearman, who is taking on a fifth Internal Combustion Engine, turbocharger, exhaust, and MGU-K, and as those components all exceed the permitted amount per season, he will start at the back of the grid. Yet for his teammate, former New York Giants defensive end Michael Strahan, Tuck missed one accolade that left his resume short of being perfect. To Strahan, Tuck deserved that honor, which was handed to quarterback Eli Manning. “One thing I will say, and I love him. We had him on the podcast. I love my guy Eli Manning. top.title: Four takeaways from Virginia’s 103-61 win against Loyola MD
top.description: The undefeated Virginia Cavaliers (7-0) secured a 42-point win over the Loyola Maryland Greyhounds (1-5) on Friday night. The 103-61 victory was not unexpected, but these non-conference games give an early look into the team’s potential for the season. Based on Friday’s 100-point game, Virginia’s crystal ball is looking pretty bright. Here are my four takeaways from the statement win. top.title: ‘Life is Too Short,’ ‘I Wish Him Nothing But the Best’ — Stephen A. Smith Addresses LeBron James Feud in Exchange With Skip Bayless
top.description: ‘Life is Too Short,’ ‘I Wish Him Nothing But the Best’ — Stephen A. Smith Addresses LeBron James Feud in Exchange With Skip Bayless Skip Bayless asked Stephen A. Smith on Friday’s episode of ESPN’s “First Take” whether he had mended his relationship with Philadelphia 76ers star LeBron James. Smith said he had not, making clear that the two had not formally reconciled. The question brought their public feud back into focus, nearly two years after the four-time NBA MVP confronted Smith courtside over his criticism of his son, Bronny James. Stephen A. Smith Explains Where He Stands With LeBron James After Their Feud Smith addressed Bayless’ question directly before explaining why he sees little reason to hold on to the disagreement. “I’m 59 years old, bro. Life is too short. I ain’t got time to be enemies with nobody,” Smith said. “I got a job to do. I wish him nothing but the best.” The disagreement began with Smith’s criticism of James’ involvement in his son’s development with the Los Angeles Lakers. On Jan. 29, 2025, Smith questioned why the veteran superstar was pushing for Bronny to remain in the NBA rather than spend more time developing in the G League. The Lakers’ 2024 second-rounder had just gone scoreless on 0-for-5 shooting in a loss to the 76ers. Smith’s comments eventually led to a courtside confrontation during the Lakers’ game against the New York Knicks on March 6. James approached Smith and told him to stop talking about his son. The sports media personality talked about the encounter in his show the following morning, acknowledging that the 22-time All-Star had confronted him as a father protecting his child. “That wasn’t a basketball player confronting me. That was a parent. That was a father,” Smith said. James later explained his side on “The Pat McAfee Show” on March 26. He said he had no issue with analysts criticizing players’ performances but objected when the discussion became personal. “Never would I ever not allow people to talk about the sport, criticize players about what they do on the court,” James said . “But when you take it, and you get personal with it, it’s my job to not only protect my damn household but protect the players.” Smith revisited the confrontation in April 2026 during an appearance on Logan Paul’s “Impaulsive” podcast. He described James’ approach as “very disrespectful” and said he felt James had wrongly assumed his criticism of Bronny was intended to get at him. He also expressed hope that the 41-year-old forward would win a championship with Philadelphia. James and the 76ers entered Friday at 13-3, tied for the best record in the NBA. nigeria.description: By Chioma Gabriel, Editor, Special Features It is often said that women are a necessary evil, a desirable calamity and a domestic peril. It all depends on where one is standing. In traditional African societies, a woman’s place was said to be in the kitchen, from where she was expected to work her way into her husband’s heart through his stomach. Women were traditionally expected to be seen but not heard. They were like shadows trailing their husbands, with little or no opportunity to express opinions on matters affecting the family and society. They were often regarded as acquired possessions whose primary responsibilities were to bear children and provide labour on the farms. They had little or no say in the scheme of things. A similar pattern appears in some biblical accounts, where headcounts excluded women and children. When Jesus fed the 5,000 and the 4,000, the recorded figures referred to the men, with women and children excluded from the count. In the early Christian community, Paul’s instruction required women to remain silent in church and ask their husbands questions at home. Although interpretations of this passage differ among Christian scholars, it has historically been cited to support restrictions on women’s public religious participation. Despite these historical and cultural limitations, women have, in different ways, exercised considerable influence over men, including their husbands. Eve persuaded Adam to eat the forbidden fruit after the serpent tempted her in the Garden of Eden. Jezebel manipulated her husband, King Ahab, and orchestrated the murder of Naboth to acquire his vineyard. nigeria.title: Nefer introduces marketplace to make peer-to-peer currency exchange more secure for Nigerians
nigeria.description: * The new feature allows users to buy and sell currencies with other users on the Nefer platform, with funds held in escrow during transactions. Nefer Remittance , a financial technology company facilitating payments and currency exchange between Nigeria and Canada, has introduced Nefer Marketplace, a new feature that enables users to buy and sell currencies directly with one another within its platform. The launch addresses a familiar challenge for Nigerians who regularly need foreign currencies for international payments, education, business transactions, travel and other financial commitments: finding reliable people to exchange money with. For many users, peer-to-peer currency exchange has traditionally happened through WhatsApp groups, social media communities and personal referrals. While these informal networks may offer access to buyers and sellers, they often lack structured transaction processes, adequate accountability and mechanisms for resolving disputes when transactions go wrong. Nefer Marketplace seeks to provide an alternative by bringing peer-to-peer currency trading into a structured digital environment. Unlike informal arrangements where buyers and sellers transfer funds directly to one another, Nefer Marketplace incorporates an escrow mechanism. Funds are held by Nefer during the transaction, providing an additional layer of protection while the parties complete the exchange in accordance with the platform’s transaction process. This means users do not have to rely solely on personal trust or the promises of an unknown seller when arranging a currency exchange. Making Currency Exchange More Accessible The introduction of Marketplace builds on Nefer’s existing services, which help customers move money between Nigeria and Canada. business.title: Researchers Publish Security Analysis of Bitcoin’s Post-Quantum SHRINCS Proposal
business.description: Bitcoin Magazine Researchers Publish Security Analysis of Bitcoin’s Post-Quantum SHRINCS Proposal Several researchers have published a 131-page security analysis of SHRINCS, a proposed post-quantum signature scheme for Bitcoin, and are asking the wider community to look for flaws in it. Researcher Mikhail Kudinov announced the first version Thursday in a thread on X, saying the paper reduces SHRINCS’ security to the properties of its underlying hash function. The analysis, dated Nov. 18, estimates classical security of 121.4 to 122.7 bits for SHRINCS, though those figures rest on assumptions that include three unproven conjectures. Kudinov said the work is not finished. The team is still working on a new analysis of a property called SM-DSPR, whose bound has so far been conjectured, and on tightening a reprogramming step and improving a bound against quantum attackers. How SHRINCS works SHRINCS is a hash-based scheme, meaning its security rests on hash functions rather than the elliptic curve math behind today’s Bitcoin signatures. It places two designs under one key: a stateful part built on FXMSS with WOTS+C, and a stateless fallback built on SLH-DSA. Because both use the same hash function, Kudinov said, the proof has to cover both. Signature size is the main cost. Under the draft proposal, stateful SHRINCS signatures run from 548 to 4,619 bytes, while the stateless fallback is 5,777 bytes. Schnorr signatures on Bitcoin today are 64 bytes, and ECDSA signatures typically come in around 71. Signatures take up scarce block space, so larger ones mean fewer transactions per block. The risk of a stateful signature The compact stateful path carries a danger. It relies on one-time keys, and if a wallet accidentally reuses one, an attacker can forge a signature for that address and steal the funds. Wallet software therefore has to track the state of every key. The stateless path avoids the problem, but at a much larger size. Jonas Nick, Blockstream’s director of research, told Isabel Foxen Duke, head of the MARA Foundation, on MARA Foundation TV that wallets must automatically fall back to the stateless path whenever a state counter could be compromised. “It needs to be impossible for the user to behave in a way that this catastrophic event happens,” he said. “Wallet developers need to deal with this stateful component correctly.” Nick also warned that heavy use of the larger signatures would weigh on the network. “We don’t know what the fee market will look like once we have these very big signatures,” he said. “And it’s not just the fee market, it’s also just fewer transactions fit into a block, meaning fewer people can use Bitcoin. He was so convinced that I wondered whether a manual somewhere explained how men were manufactured. According to him, men were created to be strong, endure pain and keep their emotions to themselves. That was simply how they were made. “So, because you’re a man, you’re not supposed to feel hurt, fear or disappointment?” I disagreed. He insisted that showing emotions was not in a man’s nature. Who made that rule? Who decided that men could experience pain but must never be seen expressing it? At what point did being a man become synonymous with pretending that everything was fine? The conversation wilted, but it has stayed with me, perhaps because my friend wasn’t expressing an unusual opinion. He was repeating a stereotype many of us have heard all our lives: “Boys don’t cry.” “Be a man.” “Man up.” Three little expressions, and somewhere between being told to be strong and learning to say “I’m fine,” I wonder how many men have forgotten what it feels like to be heard. A father who leaves home before sunrise and returns exhausted, burdened by the weight of school fees, rent, and family expectations. We had reconnected after a long time and started seeing each other more often, especially after I resumed work following an accident I was involved in. He gradually became part of my daily routine. Whenever I went to work, he would come to pick me up from the office, and we would go home together. In many ways, he looked out for me and made sure I got home safely. We started talking more. We would discuss life, share experiences and occasionally open up about things happening in our individual lives. There was also an emotional dimension to our friendship. He was interested in me romantically, I realised, but I didn’t feel the same way. I tried to understand my feelings, but the truth was that I simply wasn’t in love with him. I couldn’t manufacture feelings that weren’t there. Then I heard that he passed away. My first reaction, strangely, was guilt. I began asking myself: Was I a good friend to him? Was I kind enough? Was I considerate? Did I treat him well? Could I have done something differently? I caught myself wondering whether I should have given him a chance . Perhaps I should have allowed him to love me. But then would I have done that out of genuine affection or simply out of pity? And would that have been fair to either of us? My understanding is that not returning someone’s romantic feelings does not mean we cannot offer them genuine friendship, kindness and compassion. I didn’t owe him romantic love, but I could have been a good friend. That has stayed with me. Beyond the guilt, there was another question I couldn’t get out of my head: Why did God allow us to reconnect? Why, after such a long time, did our paths have to cross again? entertainment.description: Report identifies next SME digitization opportunity: connecting payments with day-to-day business management. 94% of SMEs surveyed find an all-in-one payment and business solution appealing, yet only 29% currently use one, pointing to untapped demand for tools that connect payments with business management. Integrated payment and business solutions can give financial institutions a more holistic view of SME cash flow and support more tailored financing solutions over time. Small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Nigeria have largely moved beyond the first stage of digital payment adoption, but a productivity gap remains. According to Visa’s new survey for its Pay and Get Paid 2026 report, most of the SMEs surveyed in Nigeria use digital payments, showing how firmly digital commerce has taken root in the country’s small business economy. However, many SMEs still manage the related financial and operational tasks separately, with only 29% currently using an integrated solution that connects payments with broader business management. The report shows that financial admin and disconnected tools create friction for SMEs, with surveyed businesses citing challenges in tracking outstanding invoices (14%), keeping payroll records organized (19%), and preparing financial reports (16%). These pain points reflect a disconnect between payments and the operational tasks that follow, with some businesses juggling multiple systems to keep their business running. The appetite for a more connected approach is clear. According to the report, 94% of SMEs find an all-in-one payment and business solution appealing, reflecting strong interest in tools that can bring payments and key business operations into one experience. However, adoption has yet to catch up: only 29% of SMEs currently use an integrated payment and business platform. The report points to several perception barriers that may be slowing adoption. Businesses cited that they already have manual processes that work (8%), that an integrated platform may disrupt their current way of working (8%), or that they do not trust relying on a single provider (7%). These findings suggest that broader adoption will depend on helping SMEs better understand how integrated tools can be relevant, accessible, and scalable for businesses at different stages of growth. At the same time, the experience of SMEs already using integrated solutions suggests a strong value case. The report found that Nigerian businesses using an integrated tool or platform report 93% satisfaction, with 88% reporting efficiency gains, including reductions in the time and effort required to manage their business. Beyond efficiency, integrated platforms may also create new opportunities for financial institutions to deepen SME relationships by using richer payments and business-management data to better understand cash flow patterns, support risk assessment, and potentially enable more relevant lending solutions over time. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images Darian DeVries avenged his loss to Kentucky last season with a 14-point win in the rivalry series’ ‘semi-neutral’ game at Lucas Oil Stadium. Indiana remains perfect on the season while the Wildcats fall to 4-2 with lopsided losses to both high major programs they’ve seen this year. Indiana built an early lead in the game before Milan Momcilovic single-handedly brought Kentucky back from the dead. His 22-point first half was enough to kill Indiana’s momentum and give Kentucky a two point lead heading into halftime. DeVries knew that the key to the second half would be slowing him down and his group came out and did just that. Momcilovic didn’t make a three in the entire second half and Indiana finally built the lead that eluded them early in the game, eventually winning 90-76. Here are three observations from the game: Bryce Lindsay It’s not often that your most important player is a bench guy, but Bryce Lindsay is looking like the best sixth-man in the country and has been a huge difference-maker for Indiana’s perfect start. It starts with his willingness to come off the bench. Lindsay started all 31 games at Villanova last season and clearly has the ability to be a high-major starter. Whatever the conversation was to get him to accept this role at Indiana, the fit is a testament to both he and DeVries. Part of what has made this work so well is that he tends to share the floor with one of Darren Harris or Markus Burton, allowing him to alternate between shooter and driver. sports.title: 'They should be willing to flip-flop': Mike Florio suggests Thanksgiving flex games
sports.description: Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images, NBC Sports Next week’s slate of NFL games on Thanksgiving has a lot to like about it. In keeping with tradition, the Detroit Lions and Dallas Cowboys will both host a game on Turkey Day, while the third, rotating primetime game will be hosted by the Buffalo Bills. But it’s possible that one aspect of the traditional Thanksgiving Day schedule is due for a change. The Lions are always the early game on Thanksgiving, while the Cowboys kickoff around 4:30 p.m. ET. The simplest reason behind this fact is time zones, but because of the relative state of both teams and the importance of their upcoming games next Thursday, Mike Florio believes the time may be right for the NFL to embrace flexing its schedule on the holiday. This year, the Lions host the Chicago Bears in a game that will have huge ramifications in the NFC North, the best division in football by a healthy margin so far this season. The Cowboys, whose defense can’t do anything, are hosting the Philadelphia Eagles, who can’t do anything on either side of the ball. While that NFC East matchup was an easy sell on paper before the start of the season, it sure looks a lot less appealing now than it did in Week 1. Florio has high expectations for the Lions-Bears game, even if it is going to start early. “I think the ratings for that game are going to be through the roof. I’m starting to think it might even be larger than the 47.7 million from last year,” Florio said, referencing the massive rating the Lions brought in with their Thanksgiving game against the Packers in 2025. “People are going to appreciate the fact that the good game is the early game. The middle game, Eagles-Cowboys, who cares? If you want to see a good, compelling, dramatic football game, that’s the one. It used to be the other way around. How many years was the Lions game just, ‘That’s what’s on TV — somebody is rolling into Detroit to beat up the Lions, it’s going to be 23–6 in the fourth quarter, let’s just get this thing over with and let’s bring out the Cowboys’? The vibe has completely shifted.” Florio argued that given the league’s broad flex privileges when it comes to its primetime schedule, a similar ability should be established to allow the league to move the better Thanksgiving game into the afternoon slot. “Frankly, they flex everything else. They should be willing to flip-flop the Lions and Cowboys games. They should be willing to say, ‘Alright we’re starting the Cowboys game at basically 12:30 p.m. ET, and we’re going to delay the Lions game.’ You give people a week, two weeks notice. We would’ve known a week or two ago that Bears-Lions is the far more compelling game. If you want to blow out the number at 4:30 p.m. ET, you put Bears-Lions in that window.” The ratings for Bears-Lions on Thanksgiving will be through the roof. He also says the intrusion into Pat Cummins’ private life has gone too far. Marsh believes a shared acknowledgement could help the sport heal and move on. Paul Marsh calls on Pat Cummins and Cricket Australia to take collective responsibility to end Sandpapergate crisis A peace deal of sorts for the Sandpapergate saga is what Paul Marsh, the chief executive of the Australian Cricketers’ Association (ACA), is now proposing. He wants every member of the 2018 touring group in South Africa, Pat Cummins and the other fast bowlers included, to stand alongside Cricket Australia (CA) and accept collective responsibility for what happened. He has stayed in regular contact with Cummins, Usman Khawaja and other players and support staff from that period, former coach Darren Lehmann among them. Out of those conversations, Marsh has concluded that an admission of shared accountability offers the group its best chance of moving forward, even if some of those on the tour continue to deny any specific knowledge of sandpaper. The proposal arrives at a delicate moment, since the dispute over who knew what, and when, has split opinion inside the game and raised awkward questions about the Australian captain himself. The current tension traces back to 2021, when Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon put their names to a joint statement, where they insisted that they had no prior knowledge of sandpaper being “taken onto the field”. Cummins has since doubled down on his position, and he now says he had no knowledge of any ball tampering, either before the tour or during it. Those claims have now been challenged by Khawaja, David Warner, Chadd Sayers and Cameron Bancroft, and their accounts have fed a growing credibility problem for Australian cricket. The situation is made more sensitive by the ACA’s own makeup, because Khawaja is a current director of the body that Marsh leads. Cummins is a former director, and so is his manager, Neil Maxwell. The 103-61 victory was not unexpected, but these non-conference games give an early look into the team’s potential for the season. He and Chance Mallory make up one of Virginia’s most dangerous pairings. Mallory’s 10 points and six assists were the perfect complement. Plus, they hit a perfect 8-of-8 from the line. If it weren’t for their 18 turnovers, you could say Loyola played a solid game. But that speaks to just how good Virginia really is. sports.title: ‘Life is Too Short,’ ‘I Wish Him Nothing But the Best’ — Stephen A. Smith Addresses LeBron James Feud in Exchange With Skip Bayless
sports.description: ‘Life is Too Short,’ ‘I Wish Him Nothing But the Best’ — Stephen A. Smith Addresses LeBron James Feud in Exchange With Skip Bayless Skip Bayless asked Stephen A. Smith on Friday’s episode of ESPN’s “First Take” whether he had mended his relationship with Philadelphia 76ers star LeBron James. Smith said he had not, making clear that the two had not formally reconciled. The question brought their public feud back into focus, nearly two years after the four-time NBA MVP confronted Smith courtside over his criticism of his son, Bronny James. Stephen A. Smith Explains Where He Stands With LeBron James After Their Feud Smith addressed Bayless’ question directly before explaining why he sees little reason to hold on to the disagreement. “I’m 59 years old, bro. Life is too short. I ain’t got time to be enemies with nobody,” Smith said. “I got a job to do. I wish him nothing but the best.” The disagreement began with Smith’s criticism of James’ involvement in his son’s development with the Los Angeles Lakers. On Jan. 29, 2025, Smith questioned why the veteran superstar was pushing for Bronny to remain in the NBA rather than spend more time developing in the G League. The Lakers’ 2024 second-rounder had just gone scoreless on 0-for-5 shooting in a loss to the 76ers. Smith’s comments eventually led to a courtside confrontation during the Lakers’ game against the New York Knicks on March 6. James approached Smith and told him to stop talking about his son. The sports media personality talked about the encounter in his show the following morning, acknowledging that the 22-time All-Star had confronted him as a father protecting his child. “That wasn’t a basketball player confronting me. That was a parent. That was a father,” Smith said. James later explained his side on “The Pat McAfee Show” on March 26. He said he had no issue with analysts criticizing players’ performances but objected when the discussion became personal. “Never would I ever not allow people to talk about the sport, criticize players about what they do on the court,” James said . “But when you take it, and you get personal with it, it’s my job to not only protect my damn household but protect the players.” Smith revisited the confrontation in April 2026 during an appearance on Logan Paul’s “Impaulsive” podcast. He described James’ approach as “very disrespectful” and said he felt James had wrongly assumed his criticism of Bronny was intended to get at him. SEE ALSO: ‘All-Time Melodramatic Flopper’ – Skip Bayless Rips LeBron James After 76ers Star’s Viral Airball The ESPN star has since said he no longer holds a grudge against James.On Friday, he reiterated that he does not hate James and wants to cover the final stretch of his NBA career without carrying the dispute forward. He also expressed hope that the 41-year-old forward would win a championship with Philadelphia. James and the 76ers entered Friday at 13-3, tied for the best record in the NBA. technology.title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
technology.description: Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve. The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model. Security breaches, prompt theft, and privacy violations To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible. technology.title: Watching as a giant star swallowed its neighbor and exploded
technology.description: In the Andromeda Galaxy, a giant star about seven times as massive as the Sun spent nearly a decade slowly swallowing its much smaller companion. The process, known as common envelope evolution, was proposed in the 1970s to explain how some of the tightest pairs of stars in the Universe form, but no one had ever caught it in the act. In a new Nature study, astronomers led by Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University, finally witnessed the entire spectacle from the decades before it began to the eruption that ended it in late 2025. “It lasts for a few years, maybe a few decades,” Karambelkar said. “Stars evolve on time scales of millions of years. So, it's really like a blip on the entire cosmic time scale.” Shared envelopes Some pairs of stars orbit so close to each other that they could not have formed at that distance, so their orbits must have shrunk. Common envelope evolution is the leading explanation for that shrinkage. When one star in a binary grows old, it expands into a giant, and its outer layers can engulf its companion. The two then share a single, loosely bound envelope of gas. As the engulfed star drags through it, it loses orbital energy to friction and spirals inward. Depending on how much of the envelope gets lost, the pair either ends up in a much tighter orbit or merges. Read full article Comments

CTIA told the FCC in an October 1 filing : The pilot test was limited in the number of micro-jammers deployed, the spectrum bands they were authorized to jam, and the power levels at which they were permitted to operate. Even with these constraints, the micro-jamming system blocked 911 calls, interfered with public safety and other communications, and caused interference that impacted wireless network infrastructure up to two and a half miles away. At the same time, the pilot results show substantial gaps in jamming the targeted “contraband” devices, with testing scenarios in outdoor inmate recreation areas showing failure rates—meaning “contraband” device call completion—in one-half to two-thirds of call attempts. science.title: What is the Riemann hypothesis and why is its solution so monumental?
science.description: Bernhard Riemann set out a problem mathematicians have been trying solve for more than a century The Granger Collection/Alamy The cadence of prime numbers has a pattern; it isn’t simply chaos. Mathematician Bernhard Riemann suspected this was the case, but he never proved it conclusively, and his mathematical successors have spent more than a century trying to demonstrate that he was right. The Riemann hypothesis may now be proven , and it could reveal the most basic structure of our number system, while also opening the door for a new understanding of the vast world of mathematical functions. Read more Mathematicians and AI in behind-the-scenes battle over what’s true In 1859, Riemann made a casual remark about a mathematical function in his memoir, qualifying a statement about it as “very probably” true. The fact that he never proved it more definitively has held the world of mathematics in suspense ever since, and the “Riemann hypothesis” became the field’s most famous and stubbornly unsolved problem – until now. A new AI-assisted proof by Levent Alpöge at Anthropic may have just ended a whole era of mathematics by confirming Riemann’s hunch from nearly 200 years ago. “This result, if true, will be the culmination of a struggle thousands of mathematicians have attempted in the past,” says Christopher Hughes at the University of York in the UK. The proof of the Reimann hypothesis is also one of the Clay Mathematics Institute ’s Millennium Prize Problems, each of which comes with a $1 million prize for a solution. Advertisement The Riemann hypothesis has loomed so large over mathematicians for decades because it concerns mathematics’ most simple yet hard-to-understand objects: prime numbers . These are numbers that aren’t divisible by any number other than 1 and themselves, and any number can be built by multiplying primes. In this way, primes are the bones of all systems of numbers; everything is built on top of them. But how primes are distributed among all numbers is, on the face of it, unpredictable. This is where Riemann made an intervention. He hypothesised that the way primes are spaced throughout the number line can be inferred from another set of numbers, now tied to a mathematical function called the Riemann zeta function. These numbers are complex – so each is actually a pair of numbers, one called real and one called imaginary – and when they are plugged into the Riemann zeta function, the function spits out zero. Confusingly, these numbers that result in a zero from the function are called “non-trivial zeros”. Riemann discovered that summing over a sequence of these complex numbers allowed him to predict the distribution of primes up to a certain high number. Effectively, he came upon a formula that could make sense of primes’ seemingly random appearances among numbers. science.title: Don't turn the moon into the Wild West, scientists warn
science.description:
Tereza is a London-based science and technology journalist, aspiring fiction writer and amateur gymnast. Originally from Prague, the Czech Republic, she spent the first seven years of her career working as a reporter, script-writer and presenter for various TV programmes of the Czech Public Service Television. She later took a career break to pursue further education and added a Master's in Science from the International Space University, France, to her Bachelor's in Journalism and Master's in Cultural Anthropology from Prague's Charles University. She worked as a reporter at the Engineering and Technology magazine, freelanced for a range of publications including Live Science, Space.com, Professional Engineering, Via Satellite and Space News and served as a maternity cover science editor at the European Space Agency.

Researchers are calling for a moratorium on industrial exploitation of the moon, fearing that rapid development could cause irreversible environmental damage and destroy invaluable scientific material. Both China and the U.S. are pushing forward with plans to establish permanent human settlements on the moon by the end of the next decade. Commercial players want to build businesses supporting these future explorers by mining for resources such as water , construction materials, industrial metals and rare earth minerals. However, some scientists argue that a temporary ban on lunar industrialization is necessary to allow regulations to catch up and limit what can be allowed in order to prevent a moon rush from destroying the pristine lunar environment. Two such researchers are Florian Rabitz, a professor of climate and technology governance at Vilnius University in Lithuania, and Xiao-Shan Yap, an assistant professor of Earth-space sustainability at Utrecht University in the Netherlands. In a piece published last month in the journal Global Environmental Politics , the pair call for "robust international regulations" and "broad and inclusive deliberation" to allow the global community to carefully consider the impact of economic activities on the moon. In addition to the threat to the scientifically priceless lunar landscape, the researchers also object to the colonization of the moon by a small number of powerful players — namely China, the U.S. and their respective close allies. "With the moon it's absolutely clear that whoever is doing the big infrastructure work is going to be asserting their position, including by defining their own exclusive territories," Rabitz said in a statement . "That shouldn't be the Wild West." Rabitz pointed out that, although the United Nations' 1967 Outer Space Treaty prevents individual nations from appropriating the moon, Earth's natural satellite and its valuable resources are unlikely to remain truly neutral territory if its exploitation is going to be led by a small number of powerful nations.

science.title: GTA hasn't gone to space (yet), but these sci-fi games can offer you a life of crime among the stars
science.description: GTA 6 has only just come out, and it's already taken the world by storm and positioned itself as one of the greatest games of all time . Great news for gamers, but what about sci-fi fans? To this day, Rockstar Games sadly hasn't embraced sci-fi with any of its open-world games (save for those UFO Easter eggs). It doesn't seem likely they'll journey to the stars anytime soon — you can't really do cutting societal satire about space — but that doesn't mean there aren't GTA-adjacent sci-fi adventures set in outer space. The frustrating thing is that no one has exactly cracked that pitch yet. Non-linear games set in outer space tend to be either too ambitious, like No Man's Sky, or too focused on specific experiences like space combat, like Star Wars: Squadrons. The end result is a roster of great sandboxes that let us journey to different star systems, but no game that dares to explore a criminal fantasy with the level of depth and opportunities seen in the last few Rockstar games. With new hardware powering far more complex open-world games, it's only a matter of time before "GTA in space" is a real thing. For now, there are some space games that let us explore sci-fi worlds, roleplaying as criminals and outlaws amongst the stars. Roleplaying a space outlaw (Image credit: Bethesda Softworks) Massive space RPGs like Starfield and The Outer Worlds 2 offer vast playgrounds you can explore and redefine through your actions. The lawful path is the obvious choice if you'd like to save the galaxy, but a life of crime awaits those who tire of the heroics. Starfield even has a "new game plus" mechanic baked into the player's journey, encouraging experimentation and living different lives, so if you stick with the divisive space RPG, the criminal life is all but unavoidable. And in traditional Bethesda fashion, you're not rushed to the next "main" objective, so if you want to become the most dangerous space criminal in the Settled Systems, you'll be supported by the mechanics and systems. You can always get back to saving the galaxy when you feel like it. (Image credit: Xbox Game Studios) The Outer Worlds 2 is another option if you want to become a star-surfing scoundrel. It might not be as absurdly expansive as Starfield, but Obsidian's whole deal has always been freedom of choice and roleplaying, so you can bet this humorous sequel also lets the protagonist become a bit of an a-hole. The main story already sets you in a collision course with corporate interests, too. Like in Mass Effect and other classic space RPGs, it's your choice to be either a goody-two-shoes or an edgy maniac, and I won't lie: the second option is usually more entertaining. Last but not least, there's a third game that also has enough going on to support a GTA-inspired fantasy in outer space: No Man's Sky . science.title: Trouble at Mars: NASA's Perseverance rover, Odyssey orbiter halt science work due to glitches
science.description: null Two of NASA's Mars explorers are sidelined by glitches at the moment. The Perseverance rover and Mars Odyssey orbiter have stood down from science work due to technical problems, NASA announced on Thursday (Nov. 19). Perseverance has been sidelined by an antenna issue, and the venerable Odyssey is dealing with a balky reaction wheel. NASA hopes both can get back to work at Mars by the end of November. Communication issues for Perseverance Perseverance landed inside Mars' Jezero Crater in February 2021, tasked with assessing the area's potential to support past life and with collecting dozens of samples for future return to Earth. It has done all this and more. The Perseverance team has determined that Jezero hosted a potentially habitable lake billions of years ago. And the car-sized rover has found a wealth of complex organic compounds in Martian rock, some of which might themselves be signs of life (though assessing this hypothesis fully will likely require bringing Perseverance's samples to Earth for analysis, scientists stress). In addition, Perseverance just set a new distance record for off-Earth driving, rolling past the mark set by its smaller cousin, NASA's Opportunity rover (28.06 miles, or 45.16 kilometers). Perseverance broke that record on Oct. 11. Just 19 days later, however, the mission team noticed a problem: The rover's main UHF downlink radio — which it uses to send information home to Earth, via data-relay satellites in Mars orbit — failed to send its usual "heartbeat" pings to the main computer. Perseverance detected this problem autonomously and reacted as it was programmed to do: The six-wheeled robot switched to its backup UHF radio and went into a protective "safe mode," shutting down all non-essential systems. The rover team recovered Perseverance from safe mode but soon noticed another issue: "The backup UHF radio was transmitting at about half of its expected power output," NASA officials wrote in an update on Thursday . Perseverance's handlers have stopped using that backup radio as well; the rover is now communicating with Earth directly (without the help of relay orbiters), sending signals to NASA's Deep Space Network dishes via its high-gain antenna. This pathway features lower data rates, and the mission team wants to prioritize the delivery of diagnostic information. So they've paused Perseverance's science work, which includes observations by its various cameras. The glitch may be disappointing to devoted Perseverance fans, many of whom have already noticed that the mission website hasn't uploaded any new raw images since Nov. 7 . But there's no reason to panic, according to NASA. "The rover is stable and communicating with the team," agency officials wrote in Thursday's update. "The team is hopeful the rover could return to science by the end of November, and NASA will provide further updates in the future as the team works the issue." science.title: There's an impostor hiding in the Hyades star cluster. Can you spot it?
science.description: null For years I looked at Taurus and saw something perfectly sensible. There was the Hyades, the big V-shaped cluster that forms the bull's face, with Aldebaran, noticeably brighter and more orange than the other stars, the dominant star. Every diagram reinforced the arrangement — Aldebaran was the eye of Taurus, the Hyades made the face, and in my head they became one object. Then I discovered that Aldebaran has nothing to do with the Hyades. I remember going outside afterward and looking again, half expecting the deception to become obvious now that I knew. It didn't. Aldebaran still looked completely at home among the other stars . The difference is hidden in the one dimension our eyes judge poorly when we look into space — depth. Aldebaran is about 65 light-years away, while the Hyades are roughly 150 light-years distant. The orange eye of Taurus is a foreground star that happens to lie almost exactly along our line of sight toward the Hyades. This fact exposes one of the most convincing tricks in stargazing. The night sky looks flat, and our brains are extremely willing to believe it. But it has incredible depth — and when you can see parts of the night sky in 3D, that's when you begin to appreciate that you're not looking at a flat map. Instead, you begin to see our cosmic neighborhood as it really is. By appreciating depth, you learn its geography. What's happening and when to look Aldebaran, the brightest star in the constellation of Taurus. (Image credit: Christophe Lehenaff via Getty Images) Taurus is now easy to find from the Northern Hemisphere during the evening. Once it's dark, look east for a small, tight knot of stars — the Pleiades open cluster (M45) — and then look nearby for a much larger V-shaped arrangement. That V is the Hyades, with unmistakably orange Aldebaran apparently sitting on one arm. Aldebaran's name is derived from the Arabic Al Dabarān, meaning "the follower," because it appears to trail the Pleiades across the night sky. The Hyades is a real physical group of stars — an open cluster — that formed together and moves through our galaxy together. About 153 light-years away, the Hyades is the nearest open star cluster to Earth. The name means "the rainmakers" because their rising and setting times in the ancient Greek sky coincided with wet weather. The stars in the Hyades are of a similar age — and mostly sun-like stars, or similar — so astronomers can tell that they all formed together in the same nebula . Orange-red star Aldebaran — the 14th-brightest star in the night sky — is the interloper, sitting less than half as far away from the sun . science.title: Could an ancient solar eclipse rewrite Egyptian history?
science.description: null The solar system is a clock that can be run in both directions. On Aug. 2, 2027, that clock will bring the moon's dark central shadow — a path of totality — back to Egypt. A t otal solar eclipse will sweep across the country , passing directly over Luxor and plunging some of ancient Egypt's greatest surviving monuments into darkness. Totality will begin in Luxor at approximately 1:02 p.m. EEST and last 6 minutes 22 seconds, according to Time and Date . We know when it will happen because we can calculate the motions of Earth and the moon centuries in advance. But run the same celestial clock backward and eclipses become one of nature's most precise timestamps. Astronomers can reconstruct where the moon's shadow fell thousands of years ago, even when nobody left a record of it. When an ancient text reliably describes an eclipse, it can anchor a moment in history to a specific place and time. Did an eclipse rewrite the Pyramid Age? Pharaoh Shepseskaf's huge rectangular tomb at South Saqqara (Image credit: Jon Bodsworth - www.egyptarchive.co.uk) We know from astronomical calculations that eclipses crossed Egypt long before anyone left an identifiable written record of one. On April 1, 2471 B.C., a total solar eclipse swept across northern Egypt during the age of the great pyramid builders. In research published in 2025, archaeoastronomer Giulio Magli at the Polytechnic University of Milan proposed that the eclipse may help explain why Pharaoh Shepseskaf broke with tradition and built a huge rectangular tomb at South Saqqara instead of a pyramid. It's a tantalizing hypothesis, but no surviving Egyptian text records the eclipse. Astronomers can calculate that an eclipse happened, but using it as a historical timestamp requires evidence that someone actually saw it and recorded it. That's where an eclipse almost 1,300 years later becomes particularly intriguing. Is the oldest recorded eclipse hidden in the Bible? science.description: null Last month, the U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) released a chilling and info-packed report judging the scope and breadth of threats posed by the nation's adversaries in space. The new report focuses on China , Russia and the emerging space powers of Iran and North Korea. It looks at what's happening in Earth orbit and beyond, including cislunar space, the region between our planet and the moon . The report — the 2026 edition of "Challenges to Security in Space" — is the third iteration of the DIA's unclassified intelligence assessment on space-related challenges and threats to U.S. national security, as well as the extent to which space is treated internationally as a warfighting domain . Information within the report, which you can read here , is current as of July 2026. DIA's mission is to provide intelligence on foreign militaries to help prevent wars, and win the ones that are fought. Up-front finding The report's up-front finding is that China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea are developing, testing, deploying and using space capabilities "in a way that threatens the security of all space systems and their associated space benefits." Indeed, China and Russia are developing "a formidable spectrum" of offensive capabilities to degrade or destroy space services of other countries, from kinetic destruction to sophisticated jamming and cyber operations. The DIA report also notes that "the production of cheaper, smaller, and simpler satellites , which are faster to develop and deploy, along with the expansion of commercially available launch services, are driving the rapid integration of commercial space alternatives to support national security." While space commercialization is making previously government-centered space services widely available to interested parties, the DIA report adds, that availability also includes state and non-state actors with malign interests. There are a range of threats to space-based services, both commercial and military. Some are reversible, while others are not. science.description: The Riemann hypothesis describes a pattern within the prime numbers ROBERT BROOK/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Alamy A mathematician at AI company Anthropic claims to have discovered, and verified with formalisation, a proof of the Riemann hypothesis – one of the most infamous and thorny problems in all of mathematics. The Riemann hypothesis was first put forward in 1859 by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It proposes an origin for the prime numbers, namely that they follow a certain pattern. The question is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, which will award a $1 million prize for an accepted solution. Read more OpenAI has dumped 722 maths papers – now it must clean up the mess Levent Alpöge at Anthropic published a statement today claiming to have solved the problem with the aid of Anthropic’s Claude AI. Advertisement “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis,” writes Alpöge. “It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.” In August, Anthropic announced previous work on the Riemann hypothesis , but that stopped short of a full proof. Alpöge hasn’t published a human-readable version of the proof, saying it would be “obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of ‘slop'”, though he says an unpublished version ran to more than 250,000 pages. Instead, Alpöge has released a version of the proof written in Lean, a computer code mathematicians use to mechanically verify proofs as a series of logical steps in a process called formalisation. science.title: ISS astronauts look down on the snow-capped Himalayas | Space photo of the day for Nov. 20, 2026
science.description: null A snapshot of the Himalayas captured from aboard the ISS. (Image credit: CSA/Joshua Kutryk) The Himalayas tower below the clouds, capped in icy snow in new snapshots captured from aboard the International Space Station . What is it? Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk was looking out one of the windows aboard the space station when the most incredible view came into focus — and thankfully he had a camera handy and was able to capture these striking scenes of the Himalayas from space. Above the mountain range, fluffy clouds hang in the atmosphere. Below, the expansive Himalayas are covered in bright snow and ice, which looks somehow both white and blue at the same time as the bright sunlight streaks across the breathtaking expanse. This frosty winter scene showcases the mountain range from orbit, from about 250 miles (400 kilometers) above Earth's surface. But even from this distance, the magnitude of this mountain range is palpable. The Himalayas stretch across five different countries including Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan. And the Himalayas include some of the highest mountain peaks on planet Earth, including Mount Everest. Himalayas 🗻 https://t.co/IzGzu20H4Q November 17, 2026 Why is it incredible? From orbit around Earth, you might expect even the largest landmarks on our planet to appear miniscule. But somehow, in these photographs snapped by Kutryk during NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 mission , even from hundreds of miles above our planet you can really see and feel the immense scale of this mammoth mountain range. It's unclear exactly where above the mountain range these photographs were taken, but it is always amazing to think that within these sweeping landscapes are people living their lives, likely unaware that an astronaut is taking in the beauty of their home. Perhaps somewhere hidden under the clouds in one of Kutryk's photographs are hikers climbing up the side of Mt. Everest, completing their own bucket list adventure as the astronauts watching from above complete theirs.

science.title: I got to tour SpaceX's Starfactory facility in Starbase, Texas, and what I saw blew my mind
science.description: null STARBASE, Texas — I just finished covering the Starship Flight 15 mission, and SpaceXs incredible launch tower catch of the returned Ship 42 spacecraft isn't the only thing over the weekend that left me speechless. The morning of the launch (Nov. 13), SpaceX invited media on a tour of Starbase's Starfactory facility, where it manufactures and assembles both stages of its massive Starship rocket - an unprecedented behind-the-scenes look at the production and scale of SpaceX's operations, and a glimpse of things to come as Starship notches more and more milestones the more it flies. For some context, the five-story-tall Starfactory spans approximately 1 million square feet (~93,000 meters), with operations split between Starship's Super Heavy boosters and upper stage Ships, and nearly 330,000 additional square feet (30,000 square meters) of office space. SpaceX officials describe its design as one more akin to an automotive manufacturing plant than that of a typical aerospace production site, and inside, it is absolutely alive with activity. Inside Starfactory We entered through an arch-covered doorway underneath the giant "X" sign on the building's shorter face. Our media gaggle was met with curious glances as we were shown through the doors and guided onto the factory floor - few are ever able to cross that threshold outside of SpaceX employees, and our presence seemed as novel to those busy working as it was to us. Inside, we were struck with the sheer enormity of Starship's scale. Giant stainless-steel rocket parts were meticulously scattered across different subassembly stations throughout the building, with Ship nose cones, cylindrical sections and booster components all under various stages of manufacture. The sheer quantity of the hardware was staggering, and being so close to each as we walked Starfactory's throughways was an eye-opener. The exterior of SpaceX's Starfactory facility at Starbase, Texas. (Image credit: Josh Dinner/Future) Starbase is a unique partnership of privately-owned SpaceX property and publicly-accessible land and shoreline, which has created the unique ability for anyone with a mind to do so to drive right up to the the Starship launch pad to see the facilities up close (within a few hundred feet or so, which, as rockets go, is very, very close). Fully stacked, Starship stands more than 400 feet (120 meters) tall. Standing next to such a towering colossus on the pad is enough to drive home just how big the launch vehicle is, but standing next its segmented components inside Starfactory is even more humbling; like seeing one of Ship's upper aerodynamic flaps, which are each large enough when laid flat that you could park a pair of large SUVs on their faces with room to spare. science.title: Einstein was right! Scientists verify 1st image of a black hole ever captured
science.description: null An independent team of researchers has validated the first image of a supermassive black hole captured by humanity. That, in turn, verifies Einstein's greatest theory, general relativity , which first predicted the existence of black holes and what their immediate surroundings would look like. Captured by a global network of telescopes forming an interferometer called the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) and revealed to the public in 2019, the image shows the supermassive black hole at the heart of the galaxy Messier 87 (M87), located 55 million light-years away. The image of this black hole , designated M87*, with a mass around 6.5 billion times that of the sun, was an immense scientific achievement. That may lead to the question: why did it need verifying at all? Team leader and researcher with Australia's Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO), Samuel Lai explained why capturing the image of a distant black hole is so tricky. "It is like standing in your backyard and trying to take a photo of a doughnut on the moon," Lai said in a statement sent to Space.com via email. Lai and his small Australian team developed advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques to capture information about the black hole's structure and filter out interference resulting from the fact that the EHT was viewing M87* from within our planet's atmosphere. The machine-learning technique called GenDIReCT also accounted for biases introduced by combining telescopes to create an Earth-sized interferometer. "When we applied it to the original EHT dataset, we found a black hole almost identical in size and shape as the historic EHT image. Importantly, our model had no idea what a black hole looked like when we applied it to the M87 data," Lai continued. "This is the first truly independent validation of the EHT image, an important step in the scientific process." This could settle the questions of just how the final image of M87* was influenced by both atmospheric effects and the processing methods needed to reconstruct pictures from telescope data. That's not just good news for the EHT; it's good news for Einstein. Take it away Einstein Einstein published his theory of general relativity in 1915, completely reshaping how we think of gravity. General relativity suggested that objects with mass curve the very fabric of space and time, united as a single entity called spacetime. Gravity arises from that curvature. The greater the mass, the more extreme the curvature and thus the greater the gravitational influence of that object. Taking this to its extreme, scientist Karl Schwarzschild came up with a solution to the equations of general relativity that suggested an infinitesimal region with infinite mass, resulting in unrestrained curvature, a singularity. science.title: SpaceX Dragon cargo capsule heads home to Earth from the ISS
science.description: null SpaceX's 35th Dragon cargo mission has begun its journey home to Earth. The robotic Dragon capsule undocked from the International Space Station (ISS) today at 12:05 p.m. EST (1705 GMT), while the duo were flying 260 miles (418 kilometers) above western China. If all goes according to plan, the freighter will splash down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of California on Saturday (Nov. 21) at about 4:55 p.m. EST (2155 GMT). There will be no livestream for its reentry and splashdown. (Today's departure webcast did not feature live footage of the moment of undocking, as it occurred during a gap in coverage of the high-bandwidth signal needed for video.) The Dragon launched Oct. 13, on a mission called CRS-35 because it's the 35th that SpaceX has flown for NASA's Commercial Resupply Services program. The capsule arrived at the ISS on Oct. 15 , delivering more than 6,300 pounds (2,860 kilograms) of food, scientific gear and other supplies to the astronauts aboard the orbiting lab. It will bring a lot of stuff down to Earth, too. "Thousands of pounds of cargo are returning from the space station, including research samples that could advance future space exploration and improve life on Earth," NASA officials wrote in an update on Tuesday (Nov. 17). "The returning research includes a 3D-bioprinted blood vessel construct scientists used to study vascular aging and cardiovascular disease in space and on Earth ," they added. Dragon is the only cargo craft flying today that's capable of making such downward deliveries. The others — Northrop Grumman's Cygnus, Russia's Progress vehicle and Japan's HTV-X — are all expendable and burn up in Earth's atmosphere to wrap up their first and only spaceflight.
